function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
I don’t have the ability to actually clone a repository, inspect its files, or push commits back to GitHub from this environment.  
What I can do is walk you through what you’d normally do locally (or in a CI job) and give you ready‑to‑copy snippets for each of the artifacts you mentioned.  

Below is a step‑by‑step guide you can follow on your machine, plus the exact content you’ll want to place in each file.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re on Windows and don’t have SSH keys set up, you can use HTTPS instead:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the Repo & Create Artifacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Assuming the repo contains a typical Node.js app (`app.js` or `index.js`) and a `package.json`, a minimal Dockerfile would look like this:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this choice?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and includes the latest LTS Node.js release.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a clean install from `package-lock.json`.  
> * Exposing port `3000` matches the common default for Express apps; adjust if your app uses a different port.

If you prefer to use the helper function you mentioned, you could invoke it like this (in Python):

```python
from functions import create_a_docker_file

create_a_docker_file(
    directory_name=".",          # Current repo root
    base_image="node:18-alpine",
    maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>",
    expose_port=3000,
    entrypoint="node app.js"
)
```

> **Note** – The function will write a `Dockerfile` into the specified directory.  
> You can then review it before committing.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

A simple deployment + service pair for a Node.js app might be:

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # Replace with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
# k8s/service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **How to generate via the helper function**

```python
from functions import create_kubernetes_yaml_file

create_kubernetes_yaml_file(
    directory_name="k8s",
    deployment_name="nodejs-welcome",
    image_name="zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest",
    replicas=3,
    port=3000,
    service_type="LoadBalancer"
)
```

> The function will create a single YAML file (you can split it into two if you prefer).

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

Create `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Cache Docker layers
        uses: actions/cache@v3
        with:
          path: /tmp/.buildx-cache
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-${{ github.sha }}
          restore-keys: |
            ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-

      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          file: Dockerfile
          push: true
          tags: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }},zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
          cache-from: type=local,src=/tmp/.buildx-cache
          cache-to: type=local,dest=/tmp/.buildx-cache
```

> **What this does**  
> * Builds the image whenever something is pushed to `main`.  
> * Caches layers to speed up subsequent builds.  
> * Tags the image with the commit SHA and `latest`.  
> * Requires two GitHub secrets: `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` and `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN`.

---

## 3️⃣ Add Files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
```

> If you used the helper functions, they already wrote the files into the repo, so just stage them.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically trigger and build/push the Docker image.

---

### Quick Checklist

| Step | What to do | Command / File |
|------|------------|----------------|
| 1 | Clone repo | `git clone ...` |
| 2.1 | Write Dockerfile | `Dockerfile` (or `create_a_docker_file`) |
| 2.2 | Write K8s YAML | `k8s/deployment.yaml` + `k8s/service.yaml` (or `create_kubernetes_yaml_file`) |
| 2.3 | Write GitHub Actions | `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml` |
| 3 | Stage files | `git add ...` |
| 4 | Commit & push | `git commit && git push` |

---

## Final Thoughts

* **Local vs. Remote** – All the heavy lifting (cloning, inspecting, writing files) happens locally.  
* **Secrets** – Make sure you’ve added the required Docker Hub secrets to your GitHub repo settings.  
* **Testing** – Before pushing, you can run `docker build -t test-image .` locally to verify the Dockerfile works.  
* **Deployment** – Once the image is on Docker Hub, you can apply the K8s manifests with `kubectl apply -f k8s/`.

Let me know if you’d like help automating any part of this process (e.g., a script that pulls the repo, generates the files, and pushes everything).
